planting.note: Direct sow in fall or start indoors in early spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like the species, this white-flowered selection self-sows readily, so isolate it from magenta-flowered rose campion if you want seedlings to come true.

directions: Grow in poor to average, sharply drained soil in full sun, exactly as for the species; rich soil or excess water produces lax, floppy growth and shortens the plant's already brief lifespan. This white-flowered form of rose campion pairs the same felted, silvery-white foliage rosettes with pure white flowers instead of magenta, giving a cooler, more restrained look in a moon garden or white border while still lighting up at dusk. It is a short-lived perennial or biennial that persists by self-seeding, so allow a few spent flowers to set seed each year to maintain a colony, and rogue out any off-type magenta seedlings if you want to keep the planting pure white.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-4 weeks before the last frost, or divide established clumps in early spring; plants grown from seed typically flower in their second year and are otherwise long-lived and low-maintenance once established.

directions: Plant in average to lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this alpine native of the Italian and Swiss mountains resents winter wet far more than heat or drought, so gritty, fast-draining soil is essential for overwintering. Woolly, silver-gray foliage forms tidy low mounds topped in early to midsummer by branched clusters of rounded, deep rose-pink to magenta flowers held on wiry stems well above the leaves. It is more compact and longer-lived than its cousin rose campion, making it a good choice for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and the front of a sunny border. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the silver foliage neat through the rest of the season.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost or start indoors in early spring; established clumps can also be divided in early spring or immediately after flowering. Plants form persistent evergreen basal rosettes and are best left undisturbed once settled.

directions: Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this tough Eurasian native tolerates poor, rocky soils and light drought once established but declines in constantly wet ground. The common name refers to the sticky, tar-like secretion found just below the leaf nodes on the flowering stems, which traps small crawling insects. In early summer, whorled clusters of small magenta-pink to rose-red flowers rise on dark, wiry stems above tufts of narrow, glossy evergreen foliage. It suits rock gardens, gravel plantings, and the front of a border, and combines well with other lean-soil perennials. Deadhead spent flower spikes to tidy the clump; division is rarely needed since plants are long-lived.

common_name: Druett's Variegated Sea Campion (Variegated Sea Campion)

planting.note: Propagate by division or cuttings in spring, since this variegated sport is grown from vegetative starts to keep the cream leaf margins true; seed-grown plants often revert to plain green.

directions: Site in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; like the wild sea campion of coastal cliffs and shingle, this selection dislikes rich soil and winter wet far more than it minds salt spray or drought. Trailing, fleshy blue-green rosettes are edged in creamy white, giving the low mat year-round interest even before the small white, deeply notched flowers open above swollen, papery calyces in early summer. It excels tumbling over rock walls, in troughs, and in gravel gardens, and holds its variegation best in full sun. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and to remove any reverted all-green shoots.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-4 weeks before the last frost, since seed benefits from a period of cold-moist stratification for even germination; established plants can also be propagated from basal cuttings in spring. Plants may take a full season to establish before flowering well.

directions: Plant in fast-draining, gravelly or rocky soil in light shade to morning sun with protection from hot afternoon exposure, mimicking the open woodland and chaparral slopes of its native California and southern Oregon range. Sprawling stems bear sticky, hairy foliage and brilliant scarlet flowers with deeply fringed, propeller-like petals from late spring into summer, drawing hummingbirds reliably. It goes summer-dormant in the hottest, driest part of the year in its native range, so avoid overwatering dormant crowns and interplant with later-season perennials to fill the gap. Best suited to western native plant gardens and dry woodland edges rather than humid climates.
